messages.subject: double (but probably fake) QTL peak
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am running a QTL on crickets.  I have 142 males with information about song parameters.  When I run scanone I get two peaks on chromosome 1 and they are only about 2 cM apart ("normal_QTL" attached). I have run through the data checking steps recommended but nothing popped out as a likely error and all the potential errors seem to be on chromosomes other than the first.  However, if I go through the data manually and remove genotypes for 6 individuals and likely mistaken sites (i.e. if the genotypes look like A A H A A H A A A A then I remove the two Hs to be missing data so it would be A A - A A - A A A A).  If I do that then I go back to having a single QTL peak ("fixed_QTL" attached)).  I am not sure the markers are really in the wrong order as this only is 6 out of 142 individuals.  But it seems to affect the QTL mapping.  I am not sure what the best solution is here.  Basically, I have 11 markers in 3 cM which I know is too many but if I remove some of these markers in Joinmap the map has trouble assembling.  Any advice or suggestions are much appreciated.  I should also note that our genotypes were called using RNAseq data and even though I was very stringent I am not 100% certain regarding the genotypes.
Best,
Emma

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] double (but probably fake) QTL peak
messages.body_plain:
Careful curation of the marker genotypes can indeed be useful, but setting that issue aside, I wouldn't infer the presence of two QTL based on the two closely linked peaks in the LOD curve. To try to figure out whether there are two QTL or not, I'd use a two-QTL scan in the region, or I would condition on one locus and then scan for an additional locus.

LOD curves from interval mapping are calculated assuming the presence of a single QTL, and can't reliably be used to infer the presence of multiple linked QTL.

karl

messages.subject: [PACKAGE ANNOUNCEMENT]
messages.body_plain:
PACKAGE ANNOUNCEMENT:

Dear R/qtlcommunity,

I would like to announce the release of the „ABHgenotypeR” package for R.

The ABHgenotypeR package provides simple imputation, error-correction and plotting capacities for genotype data. The functions in this package were initially developed for the GBS/QTL analysis pipeline described in:

Furuta T., Reuscher S. et. al., 2016 Adapting genotyping by sequencing for rice F2 populations.

BMC Genomics (in revision)

The ABHgenotypeR package is supposed to serve as an intermediate, but independent analysis tool between the TASSEL GBS pipeline and the qtl package. As such it works directly on the output of the TASSEL GenosToABH plugin which is also one of the inputs needed for  qtl .

 ABHgenotypeR provides functionalities not found in either TASSEL or qtl in addition to visualization of genotypes as graphical genotypes. Advanced R users may utilize the full power of ggplot2 to create figures.

To install from CRAN:

install.package("ABHgenotypeR")

library(ABHgenotypeR)

or from github:

#needs "devtools"

install.packages("devtools")

library(devtools)

install_github("StefanReuscher/ABHgenotypeR", build_vignettes = TRUE)

for more information and an example workflow run:

vignette("ABHgenotypeR-vignette", package = "ABHgenotypeR")

If you find it useful or want to report a bug send an email to reus...@agr.nagoya-u.ac.jp, or contact me via github or this group.

Disclaimer: I am not affiliated with either the TASSEL or the qtl developers. The ABHgenotypeR package was developed first and foremost to aid us in genotyping our rice populations. We hope however that it will be useful to other people as well. Since we did not test this package very extensively with data from species other than rice or from a SNP caller other than TASSEL: Use at your own risk.

Also sorry for using this board for slightly off-topic things.

Greetings,

Stefan

messages.subject_clean: Mapping success and failure (like) proportion phenotypes
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm coming back to this after some time (having been collecting more data). With the first approach do you mean to run:

model <- glm (cbind(num_successes, num_failures) ~ trait, family = binomial)

where 'trait' is the probability value (i.e. a value between 0 and 1), or would you convert these (with somekind of threshold) so that the explanatory variable is categorical (i.e. a genotype).

Also I would be very grateful if you could expand on what you mean by a 'trimmed mean' for averaging the log-likelihoods.

Sorry if this is obvious, I'm still learning.

Thanks

Richard

On Wednesday, January 22, 2014 at 7:36:28 PM UTC+1, Saunak Sen wrote:
> If you have reasonably dense markers and no selective genotyping, then the simplest solution would be Haley-Knott regression.  That is you regress on the genotype probabilities between marker locations.  Run "calc.genoprob" to calculate genotype probabilities, use "pull.genoprob" to get them out as a matrix, and then use "glm" as in the code snippet you showed.
>
> data(listeria)
> listeria <- calc.genoprob(listeria, step=1, stepwidth="max")
> pr <- pull.genoprob(listeria, chr=c(5,13), omit.first.prob=TRUE, include.pos.info <http://include.pos.info>=TRUE)
>
> You can pull out imputations in the same way using "sim.geno" instead of "calc.genoprob" and "pull.draws" instead of "pull.genoprob".  There is a tricky step afterward of averaging the log-likelihoods from the different imputations.  A trimmed mean is taken, instead of a straight average. This step is explained in the Sen and Churchill (2001) paper.  I can elaborate if you wish.
>
> With regards,
> Saunak
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Mapping success and failure (like) proportion phenotypes
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

Thanks for your response. I have now done this, but I'm afraid I still have some questions.

As suggested, I calculated genotype probabilities and pulled them out:

all_data <- jittermap(all_data)

all_data <- calc.genoprob(all_data, step=1,  stepwidth="max")

pr <- pull.genoprob(all_data, omit.first.prob=TRUE)

… in addition to my phenotype data:

red_court <- pull.pheno(all_data, pheno.col = "court_mp") # ~"success"

white_court <- pull.pheno(all_data, pheno.col = "court_cp") # ~"failure"

Looking at each locus in turn, I ran the glm models:

model <- glm(cbind(red_court,white_court) ~ locus_genotypes, family = binomial)

null_model <- glm(cbind(red_white,cydno_court) ~ 1, family = binomial)

... and calculate the LOD scores for each locus as follows:

LOD<-((logLik(model) - logLik(null_model))/log(10))[1]

The attached plot compares LOD scores resulting from the binomial glm  (black line) to those from the Haley-Knott regression implemented using scanone in R/qtl. For the Haley-Knott I used the full data-set (blue line) and a reduced data set (red line) which includes individuals with 5 or greater courtship events (i.e. success + failures >= 5, ... so just those individuals with more information). By reducing the data I get a significant QTL with the hk method, but removing a lot of data doesn't seem ideal (if justified). The glm method seems to work (and makes sense in that it should take into account the amount of data collected for each individual), but the LOD score appears elevated. In terms of finding significant QTL, perhaps this isn't a problem as the LOD threshold is also elevated (which I calculated through permutation in the normal way). But, I obviously couldn't apply a 1.5-LOD interval to estimate the position of the QTL. And it looks weird.

So I'm not sure what's causing this. Perhaps I haven't calculated the LOD score properly?

Could it be that my data are over-dispersed? I would normally deal with this by using quasibinomial errors, but of course it would be hard to obtain a LOD score for these.

I'd really appreciate any thoughts you might have.

Thanks and best wishes,

Richard

messages.subject: How do I read a doubled haploid population into R QTL using the read.cross function from mapmaker type of input (R version 3.2.1 and R/QTL version 1.38-4)
messages.subject_clean: How do I read a doubled haploid population into R QTL using the read.cross function from mapmaker type of input (R version 3.2.1 and R/QTL version 1.38-4)
messages.body_plain:
The function read.cross fails to import the data (in mapmaker format) when I assign a DH population in the header of a mapmaker output. To solve this I used  “bc” in the header of the file and crosstype=”dh” in the read.cross function. The genotypes are coded as “A’ and “B” in the original file. In this way I was able to loaded the file, but based on the QTL mapping results it seems that something is going wrong with the interpolation which seems to point to wrong assumptions / scores. I obtained I large signals when using the interval mapping method and almost no signal from marker regression. The crosstype loaded is a “doubled haploid” (checked by asking for crosstype).

When I re-code the original genotype data file to A/H instead of A/B following the same procedure the results seem much more sensible, comparable results for interval mapping and marker regression.

What is this the correct way to approach a DHs (using mapmaker format), to make sure the scores are loaded correct and obtain the correct estimated effects?

messages.body_plain:
I've not seen mapmaker files for doubled haploids, so read.cross() with format="mm" only works for backcross or intercross.

I'd recommend calling it a backcross (and changing the genotype codes at the top to pretend that the BB's are hets) and then converting to doubled haploids afterwards.

mycross <- read.cross( .... )
class(mycross)[1] <- "dh"

karl

messages.subject: Number of markers in CIM analysis?
messages.subject_clean: Number of markers in CIM analysis?
messages.body_plain:
I got the following question by email and thought I'd post the question and my response, such as it is.

> I am using the CIM function in Rqtl. I am wondering what number of marker covariates to choose. My idea was to select the number based on the number of significant QTL I obtained from the scanone function, in the case of my data that would be 4 markers. Looking at several papers online it seems like people choose numbers such as 5, 10, or 15 markers. This seems like a large number and leads to a lot more significant QTL that seem untrue. I plan on using multiple qtl modeling to further test the significance of my QTL; however, I was curious what your opinion was for the choice of marker covariates.

I don't like CIM for that reason. I'd recommend using the stepwiseqtl() function.

karl
